Type host config capability flags as boolean (#37740)

The reconciler is type checked once per renderer. In renderers that
don't support a capability, its flag is exported as a literal (e.g.
`supportsHydration = false` in ReactFiberConfigWithNoHydration), so Flow
infers a literal type and reports every check of it as a constant
condition. That's a property of one build, not of the shared code, which
works with either value. We were suppressing it with
`$FlowFixMe[constant-condition]` at each use.

Annotate the flag exports as `boolean` instead, so Flow treats them as
unknown, and remove the 96 suppressions this makes unnecessary. Dead
code elimination is unaffected, because the bundler still sees the
literal value.

[DevTools] Don't remount the extension on same-document navigations (#37780)

## Summary

Fixes #37681.

Since Chrome 153, `chrome.devtools.network.onNavigated` also fires for
same-document navigations. [devtools-frontend CL
8155971](https://chromium-review.googlesource.com/c/devtools/devtools-frontend/+/8155971)
made `Page.navigatedWithinDocument` call `setInspectedURL()`, and the
DevTools extension server forwards every inspected URL change to
extensions as `onNavigated`. The callback only gets the URL. In Chrome
154 it fires for `pushState`, `replaceState` (including same-URL and
state-only calls), hash changes, intercepted Navigation API navigations
and `history.back()` within the document.

The extension treated every event as a new page. It unmounted the
panels, sent `shutdown` to the backend that was still running in the
page, and remounted. So every client-side route change lost the
selection and any in-progress Profiler recording. The remount itself was
also unreliable. The content script only says hello to the backend
manager once per document, so the re-injected backend manager depended
on timing. In some runs the page had no backend until the Components
panel was opened. In others, the new backend sent its initial tree
before the new frontend was listening.

Changes:

- **`main/index.js`, `evalScripts.js`:** only remount when the inspected
document was replaced. Keep the current instance if both of these hold:
  - it already received `extensionBackendInitialized`;
- the page still has `__REACT_DEVTOOLS_BACKEND_MANAGER_INJECTED__`. The
backend manager removes that flag when it shuts down, including on
`pagehide`, so bfcache restores still remount, and a new document never
has it.

If the check fails, it falls back to the old behavior. No new
permissions.
- **`backendManager.js`, `proxy.js`:** when the backend manager is
injected into a document whose previous backend shut down, it asks the
content script to say hello again. It now only accepts a hello as the
welcome message. Before, any message forwarded from the frontend
counted, including the old instance's `shutdown`, which could initialize
the backend while no frontend was listening.
- **`elementSelection.js`, `main/index.js`:** the remount now happens
one eval round trip later, which exposed a race. The Elements panel
selection sync could call `bridge.send` after that Bridge was shut down,
throwing "Cannot send a message through a Bridge that has been shut
down." It now only sends through the current instance's Bridge.

#37708 takes a different approach: it switches Chromium to
`webNavigation.onCommitted` and adds the `webNavigation` permission.

Firefox doesn't emit `onNavigated` for same-document navigations, so
nothing should change there, but I didn't test Firefox.

## How did you test this change?

- `yarn prettier`, `yarn linc`: pass.
- `yarn flow dom-browser`, which covers `react-devtools-extensions`, and
`yarn flow dom-node`: no errors.
- `yarn test-build-devtools --silent --no-watchman
react-devtools-extensions`: 2/2 pass. `ignoreList-test.js` builds the
extension in development and production modes. The source and www Jest
configs exclude the DevTools packages, so `yarn test` and `yarn
test-www` match no tests.
- `yarn build-for-devtools && yarn build:chrome:local`: the extension
built from this branch loads in Chrome 154.

End to end, I drove the real DevTools UI in headless Chrome
154.0.8037.93 over CDP, with an isolated profile and a React 18 SPA test
page. The Components and Profiler panels were opened with
`InspectorFrontendAPI.showPanel`. The checks were the backend agent's
identity in the page, the bridge traffic, and the rendered Components
tree. Shipped 8.0.0 compared with this branch:

| Scenario | 8.0.0 | This branch |
|---|---|---|
| Router `pushState` ×2, state-only `replaceState`, hash change,
`history.back()` within the document | Remounts on every navigation:
`shutdown` sent, new backend agent each time | Same backend agent; the
tree follows the route |
| Components panel hidden while navigating | No backend in the page
until the panel is opened | Backend stays connected |
| Profiling across two route changes | Recording lost ("No profiling
data has been recorded") | 4 commits recorded |
| Reload, link to another document, bfcache restore, cross-site
navigation | Remounts | Remounts; the tree shows the new document |

The backend-manager change on its own, with the shipped `main.js`, also
fixes the remount itself: after a same-document remount, the new backend
attaches immediately instead of waiting for the Components panel to be
opened (2/2 runs).

Closing and reopening DevTools without a reload shows an empty tree in
8.0.0 too. That's a separate issue; I closed DevTools over CDP, which
may not match a user closing it. On this branch, the next navigation
remounts and recovers it, as before.

[Flight] Fix reviving errors without stack frames in debug info (#37730)

## Summary

`serializeDebugErrorValue` outlines the error info with `objectLimit:
stack.length * 2 + 1`, but the error info object itself uses one from
that budget. With zero frames the limit is 1, so the empty `stack` array
gets deferred and goes out as `"$Y"`. The client then gets a string
placeholder where it expects an array, `buildFakeCallStack` throws on
it, and the error fails to revive. For an `AggregateError` that failure
leaves `errors` as `null`, so `AggregateError(null, ...)` throws during
parsing and the root never resolves.

Errors from Node internals (like the `ECONNREFUSED` from happy eyeballs
in the issue) have no frames, so they hit this when they show up as a
rejected I/O value or in a replayed log. Bumping the limit by one leaves
room for the stack array itself.

[ci] Reject focused Playwright tests in Flight fixture (#37757)

## Summary

Change the Flight fixture’s `forbidOnly` from `!isCI` to `isCI` to
reject `.only` on CI and allow focused debugging locally. This prevents
CI from passing while accidentally excluding other tests and matches the
existing comment.

The inverted condition dates to
[#28350](https://github.com/facebook/react/pull/28350).

## How did you test this change?

- Temporarily added `test.only()` and confirmed `CI=true yarn test`
rejects it with exit code `1`.
- Removed `.only` and ran the full Flight fixture suite from the
repository root:

```bash
yarn && yarn build && cd fixtures/flight && yarn && yarn playwright install chromium && CI=true yarn test
```

Merge pull request #126868 from GodlyDonuts:codex/skip-empty-ragged-suffixes

PiperOrigin-RevId: 997014785

Support small contiguous chunks and sub-byte chunking in TransposePlan.

1. Allow `ChooseParallelizationStrategy` to partition tensors smaller than 64 MiB when `chunk_contiguity != ChunkContiguity::kNone`. Previously, `kMinBytesPerThread` was fixed at 64 MiB (or 1 MiB for memcpy plans), which clamped `Parallelism()` to 1 for sub-64 MiB transfers even when a caller explicitly requested multiple contiguous input/output chunks for pipelined DMA staging.

2. Support `Transformation::kPackSubbyte` with `ExecuteChunk()` and `TransposeConstStride1`:
   - Support `Transformation::kPackSubbyte` directly in `TransposeConstStride1` (`inner_kernel_is_memcpy() == true`) by packing contiguous stride-1 spans via `PackIntN`, scaling outer output strides by `elements_per_byte`, and setting `loop.inc = 8 / bits_per_element_` so `PartitionLoops` only splits at byte boundaries.
   - Skip 1-iteration trivial loops in `IdentifyContiguousLoops()` so size-1 inner loops preserved by `RemoveTrivialLoops()` do not overwrite a real outer loop's `contiguity` to 2.
   - Scale `output_chunk_offset_bytes_`, `output_chunk_iteration_offsets_`, and `output_chunk_size_bytes_` by `elements_per_byte` (8 / `bits_per_element_`) in `ComputeChunkSizes()` when `transformation_ == Transformation::kPackSubbyte`.
   - For fallback sub-byte packing (`use_fallback_pack_`), allocate and zero-initialize `OutputNumElems()` bytes in `Execute()` so partial output tiles are handled safely.
   - Fall back to `use_fallback_pack_` whenever `b_is_tiled_` and `b_tiling_.back() % elements_per_byte != 0` (including `b_tiling_.back() == 1`), or when the stride-1 dimension in `B` or its tile size is not divisible by `elements_per_byte`.

3. Include `chunk_contiguity` in `TransposePlanCacheKey` equality, hashing, and lookup in `TransposePlanCache`.

### Benchmark Highlights (Before vs. After)

- **Significant improvement (`-50.9%` to `-82.9%` time/CPU reduction, `2.0x`–`5.8x` speedup) on `BM_Transpose_Pack4` with stride-1 inner dimension (`perm = {1, 0, 2}`)**:
  - `256×256×256` (`perm_1_0_2`):
    - 1 thread: `2.922 ms` → `1.434 ms` (**-50.90%**, `2.04x` faster)
    - 4 threads: `1.945 ms` → `0.458 ms` wall (`-76.46%`), `1.510 ms` → `0.347 ms` CPU (**-77.02%**, `4.35x` faster)
    - 8 threads: `1.750 ms` → `0.354 ms` wall (`-79.79%`), `1.384 ms` → `0.236 ms` CPU (**-82.92%**, `5.85x` faster)
  - `512×512×512` (`perm_1_0_2`):
    - 1 thread: `21.296 ms` → `8.813 ms` (**-58.62%**, `2.42x` faster)
    - 4 threads: `15.047 ms` → `5.363 ms` wall (`-64.36%`), `14.139 ms` → `3.955 ms` CPU (**-72.03%**, `3.57x` faster)
    - 8 threads: `13.832 ms` → `4.320 ms` wall (`-68.77%`), `13.077 ms` → `3.487 ms` CPU (**-73.34%**, `3.75x` faster)
  - **Explanation**: Previously, when `inner_kernel_is_memcpy_` was true (`pos_stride1b_in_a == pos_stride1a_in_a`) and `transformation_ == Transformation::kPackSubbyte`, `TransposePlan::Initialize()` fell back to `use_fallback_pack_ = true`, which allocated a full-tensor temporary buffer (`16 MiB` for `256³`, `128 MiB` for `512³`), copied unpacked 1-byte elements into `temp_buf`, and then ran a single-threaded `PackIntN` pass over the entire buffer. With `TransposeConstStride1<Transformation::kPackSubbyte>`, contiguous stride-1 rows are packed directly from input to output via `PackIntN` in parallel across worker threads without any intermediate buffer allocation.
- **No regressions**: All other `BM_Transpose_*` permutations (`inner_kernel_is_memcpy_ == false` or `Transformation::kNone`) and all `BM_TransposeMicroKernel` cases execute the exact same kernel paths as before when `chunk_contiguity == ChunkContiguity::kNone` (overall suite geomean `-4.30%` CPU time / `-3.71%` wall time, microkernel geomean `-0.05%`).

[XLA] Allow overriding live range analysis for Buffer Assignment

HloLiveRange for async ops is correct, but pessimistic when it comes to
context shapes. An implementation may define the async computation of
call-start.1 to execute sequentially after the async computation of
call-start.0, in which case there will be no live range overlap between the
two context shapes, hence no interference.

This change introduces `LiveRangeInterferenceOptions` to specify custom
interference rules for buffer assignment and optimizes active allocation
reuse in `FastMerge`.

`AlgebraicSimplifierVisitor::HandleDynamicUpdateSlice` folds a nested `dynamic-update-slice` on a `dynamic-slice` of the same base operand into a single `dynamic-update-slice`. The pass clamps the outer and inner start indices to their slice bounds and adds them in the outer index type. When either index uses a narrow integer type such as `s8` or `u8`, the clamp bound or the combined sum can overflow that type. An overflow wraps the start offset and causes the folded update to write to the wrong coordinates.

Check across every slice dimension that the inner clamp bound fits in the inner index element type using `primitive_util::FitsInIntegralType`. Also check that the maximum combined offset, equal to the base dimension minus the inner update size, fits in the outer index element type. Skip the folding rewrite whenever any dimension fails this check. Existing programs with wide index types are unaffected, while programs that previously suffered integer overflow now preserve the nested operations. No flags gate this bug fix.

Tests:
- `//third_party/tensorflow/compiler/xla/hlo/transforms/simplifiers:algebraic_simplifier_test` pins skipping the fold when narrow start indices would overflow.

[XLA][BufferAssignment] Split global and thread-local buffer assignment.

Sharing `AssignBuffersForComputations` between global and thread-local
computations via an `is_thread_local` flag overly complicated thread-local
buffer assignment in favor of code reuse, even though very little code was
actually shared. Thread-local computations simply assign a dedicated
allocation to each buffer and do not use call-graph post-order positions,
buffer sorting, allocation managers, operand buffer reuse, or delayed
sequential heap simulation, yet ran through that setup and branching anyway.

Split `AssignBuffersForComputations` into `AssignBuffersForGlobalComputations`
and `AssignBuffersForThreadLocalComputations`. Extract
`AssignViewOrConstantBuffer` for the only logic shared by both paths (DUS view
buffer skipping and `allocate_buffers_for_constants` handling), remove the
`is_thread_local` parameter from `AssignSpecialHloBuffer` and
`AssignSingleHloBuffer`, and return early when there are no thread-local
computations.

PR #48156: Fix sm107 cuda ptx 47982

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/48156

Fixes #47982

📝 Summary of Changes
Fixes a crash when compiling for SM107 GPUs (Compute Capability 10.7) on CUDA 12.9.
- Updated `ResolveSupportedComputeCapability` and `GetSmName` in `xla/service/gpu/llvm_gpu_backend/nvptx_backend.h` and `nvptx_backend.cc` to accept an optional `ptx_version` parameter.
- Added `GetMinimumRequiredPtxVersion` to filter out target architectures whose required minimum PTX ISA version exceeds the PTX version supported by the active CUDA version.
- On SM107 GPUs with CUDA 12.9 (PTX 8.8), target resolution now safely falls back to `sm_103f` (the Blackwell family-compatible target). On CUDA 13.4+ (PTX 9.4+), it resolves directly to `sm_107a`.
- Updated `NVPTXCompiler::CompileTargetBinary` and `NVPTXCompiler::LinkModules` in `xla/service/gpu/nvptx_compiler.cc` to pass the active PTX version to target resolution.

🎯 Justification
On SM107 GPUs with CUDA 12.9, XLA previously resolved the device compute capability to `sm_107a`. However, LLVM's NVPTX target requires PTX 9.4+ for target `sm_107a`, whereas CUDA 12.9 only supports up to PTX 8.8. Passing `sm_107a` and `+ptx88` to LLVM caused a `report_fatal_error`, aborting the process. By incorporating PTX version constraints into target resolution, XLA safely falls back to the Blackwell family-compatible target (`sm_103f`) on CUDA 12.9, enabling JAX/XLA programs to compile and execute without process failure.

🐛 Bug Fix

N/A

Added `UtilsTest.SM107FallsBackWhenPtxVersionTooLow` in `xla/service/gpu/llvm_gpu_backend/nvptx_backend_test.cc` to verify:
- SM107 (`{10, 7, kAcceleratedFeatures}`) with PTX 8.8 resolves to `sm_103f` (`{10, 3, kFamilyCompatibleFeatures}`).
- SM107 (`{10, 7, kAcceleratedFeatures}`) with PTX 9.4 resolves to `sm_107a` (`{10, 7, kAcceleratedFeatures}`).

[XLA] Fix kLt and kLe trip counts in MatchTrivialLoopTripCount

`MatchTrivialLoopTripCount` in `while_loop_analysis.cc` miscomputes trip counts for `kLt` and `kLe` loops with negative bounds or steps greater than one. In the `kLt` branch, the remainder adjustment checks `*trips < *while_cond_bound_val`, comparing the candidate trip count against the loop bound `N`. When the candidate trip count is at least `N`, such as when `N <= 0`, that check fails and undercounts by one. For zero trip `kLt` and `kLe` loops with `0 > N - init > -step`, integer division truncates toward zero and returns `1`.

Return `0` immediately when `*while_cond_bound_val <= *indvar_init_val` for `kLt` or `*while_cond_bound_val < *indvar_init_val` for `kLe`. For positive `kLt` spans, compute the trip count as `(*trips - 1) / trip_count_step + 1`. For `kLe` loops with `*trips >= 0`, compute the trip count as `CheckedAdd(*trips / trip_count_step, 1)`. Existing programs with `kLt` or `kLe` loops that have negative bounds or zero trips now receive exact static trip counts.

Tests:
- `//third_party/tensorflow/compiler/xla/hlo/analysis:while_loop_analysis_test`: `NegativeAndZeroTripCountNonUnitStep` verifies `kLt` and `kLe` trip counts for negative bounds and zero trip loops.

## Problem

`WhileLoopUnroller` substitutes wrong induction variable values when unrolling a while loop whose induction step exceeds one. `WhileLoopUnroller::IsLoopUnrollable` accepts loops with arbitrary positive step sizes through `MatchTrivialLoopTripCount`, which divides the bound difference by the step size. However, `WhileLoopConfig` did not record the induction step size. Both `UnrollInternal` and `UnrollInternalWrappedAndReturnReplacement` computed the induction value for iteration `iter` as `config.init + iter` instead of scaling `iter` by the step size.

## Change

Add `step` with a default value of `1` to `WhileLoopConfig` and populate it in `WhileLoopUnroller::IsLoopUnrollable` via `MatchTrivialLoopInductionStep`. Update `UnrollInternal` and `UnrollInternalWrappedAndReturnReplacement` to compute each unrolled iteration value as `config.init + iter * config.step` using `OverflowSafeMultiply` and `OverflowSafeAdd`.

Existing programs with unit step loops are unchanged. While loops with step sizes above one now receive the true induction value in each unrolled iteration instead of consecutive integers. No flags are added or changed.

## Tests

- `//third_party/tensorflow/compiler/xla/service:while_loop_unroller_test`: pins direct and trivial loop wrapped unrolling of a while loop with step size two accumulating the induction variable.
- `//third_party/tensorflow/compiler/xla/backends/gpu/transforms:windowed_einsum_handler_test`: updates the second unrolled iteration in `ReduceScatterF8` (which has step size two) to expect induction value `2` rather than `1`.

[XLA] Fix pad handling in AlgebraicSimplifier::AssociativeReorderDotOperator

When `use_associative_reordering` is enabled, `AssociativeReorderDotOperator` rewrites `dot(pad(x, pad_val), y)` into `dot(x, slice(y))` along contracting dimensions. This transformation has three bugs. First, it does not check that `pad_val` is zero, which silently drops nonzero padding contributions from the dot product. Second, it reorders contracting dimensions whenever any padding field is positive, even if `edge_padding_low` or `edge_padding_high` is negative, producing invalid slice bounds. Third, when checking whether a residual `pad` instruction is still required, it checks only `edge_padding_low` and `edge_padding_high` and ignores `interior_padding`. This omission drops interior padding on noncontracting dimensions and causes a shape mismatch.

Require `IsScalarConstantZero(reorder_from->operand(1))` before reordering a `pad` operand of a `dot`. Require both `edge_padding_low` and `edge_padding_high` to be nonnegative on a contracting dimension before converting its padding into a slice. Check `dim.interior_padding() != 0` when determining whether a residual `pad` instruction is needed.

Tests:
- `//third_party/tensorflow/compiler/xla/hlo/transforms/simplifiers:algebraic_simplifier_test`: `AssociativeReorderDotPadNonZeroOrInteriorPad` verifies nonzero padding values, negative edge padding, and residual interior padding on noncontracting dimensions.

Preserve constraint priority across buffer and operand layout updates

When ConstrainOrOverrideBuffersAtIndex overrides a buffer and its user operand
layout constraints at an elevated priority (existing->priority() + 1), a later
negotiated buffer layout update in BufferLayoutConstraint::UpdateLayout
previously overwrote priority_ with the incoming lower priority, and
PropagateBufferConstraintToOperands propagated at current_priority_ instead of
respecting the buffer and existing operand constraint priorities. As a result,
OperandLayoutConstraint::UpdateLayout rejected the updated output layout on
higher priority operands of instructions that cannot change layout, leaving the
instruction output and operands with mismatched layouts.

Fix this by:
- Preserving std::max(priority_, priority) in
  BufferLayoutConstraint::UpdateLayout and OperandLayoutConstraint::UpdateLayout
  (including when a new operand constraint matches the existing layout).
- Propagating with std::max(current_priority_, buffer_constraint.priority()) in
  PropagateBufferConstraintToOperands, and using at least the existing operand
  or buffer constraint priority when synchronizing operands and outputs of
  instructions that cannot change layout.
- Comparing operand indices rather than operand instruction pointers in the
  sibling loop of PropagateOperandConstraint.
- Verifying in LayoutAssignment::CheckLayouts that instructions that cannot
  change layout have matching layouts on their output and same rank array
  operands.

[XLA] Store TopK comparator order in backend_config in TopkRewriter.

#### Why:
Why this change is needed:
1. `TopkSpecializer` rewrites `"TopK"` custom calls into GPU-specific `"__gpu$TopK"` custom calls, which drop `called_computations` (`to_apply`) and only preserve `backend_config`. Storing `order` (`"TOTAL"` or `"PARTIAL"`) in `backend_config` (alongside `is_stable`) is required so `ThunkEmitter` can select between the `TOTAL`-order and `PARTIAL`-order GPU TopK kernels.
2. `TopkRewriter` (`MatchNanSafeGt`) already pattern-matches the `sort` comparator computation. Recording the resulting `ComparisonOrder` directly in `backend_config` avoids re-parsing the comparator computation in downstream passes (`TopkSpecializer`, `ThunkEmitter`).

#### Changes:
- Update `MatchNanSafeGt` in `TopkRewriter` to extract and return the matched comparator's `ComparisonOrder` (`TOTAL` or `PARTIAL`).
- Include `order = "TOTAL"` or `order = "PARTIAL"` alongside `is_stable` in `raw_backend_config_string` when creating a `"TopK"` `CustomCall` in `CreateTopKCustomCall`.
- Update `hlo_instruction_utils::GetTopKOrder` to read `order` directly from `raw_backend_config_string` (defaulting to `ComparisonOrder::kTotal`), avoiding re-parsing the comparator computation in downstream passes (`TopkSpecializer` and `ThunkEmitter`) and preserving the order on `"__gpu$TopK"` custom calls that do not attach `to_apply`.
- Update `hlo_instruction_utils_test` and `topk_rewriter_test` (including a new `TopKCustomCallPartialOrderConfig` test).

Example
```
# Before Optimization
ENTRY %TopK (x: f32[8,69632]) -> (f32[8,4], s32[8,4]) {
  %x = f32[8,69632]{1,0} parameter(0)
  ROOT %topk = (f32[8,4]{1,0}, s32[8,4]{1,0}) topk(%x), k=4, largest=true, is_stable=true
}

# after_topk-rewriter
ENTRY %TopK (x: f32[8,69632]) -> (f32[8,4], s32[8,4]) {
  %x = f32[8,69632]{1,0} parameter(0)
  %custom-call = (f32[8,4]{1,0}, s32[8,4]{1,0}) custom-call(%x), custom_call_target="TopK", called_computations={%compare-greater-than.1}, backend_config={is_stable = true, order = "TOTAL"}
  ROOT %tuple = (f32[8,4]{1,0}, s32[8,4]{1,0}) tuple(%custom-call#0, %custom-call#1)
}

# after_topk-specializer
ENTRY %TopK (x: f32[8,69632]) -> (f32[8,4], s32[8,4]) {
  %x = f32[8,69632]{1,0} parameter(0)
  %custom-call.1 = (f32[8,4]{1,0}, s32[8,4]{1,0}) custom-call(%x), custom_call_target="__gpu$TopK", api_version=API_VERSION_TYPED_FFI, backend_config={is_stable = true, order = "TOTAL"}
  %tuple.1 = (f32[8,4]{1,0}, s32[8,4]{1,0}) tuple(%custom-call.1#0, %custom-call.1#1)
  ROOT %tuple = (f32[8,4]{1,0}, s32[8,4]{1,0}) tuple(%tuple.1#0, %tuple.1#1)
}
```

[XLA] Fix while loop induction variable evaluation in HloEvaluator::HandleWhile

When `HloEvaluator::HandleWhile` partially evaluates a while loop whose input tuple contains unknown values, it folds the loop induction variable statically. It built the result literal directly from `trip_count`, ignoring the initial value and step size. Loops with a nonzero initial value or a step other than one got a wrong induction variable.

Compute the final value as `induction_var_init_value + trip_count * step_size`, matching `TryParseAndEvaluateWhileInductionVar`. The arithmetic is done in `uint64_t`, so overflow wraps the same way the narrower integer induction variable would instead of being signed overflow undefined behavior.

Partial evaluation of static loops now yields the correct induction variable. No flags are added or changed.

Tests:

Add chunked staging for host-device transfers in PJRT StreamExecutor.

In Confidential Computing mode, host-to-device and device-to-host transfers are staged through pinned host memory. Large transfers previously required allocating a single staging buffer matching the full transfer size, which could lead to host memory exhaustion or fragmentation.

This change splits all staged transfers into fixed-size chunks (defaulting to 16 MiB and configurable via XLA_PJRT_GPU_CC_STAGING_CHUNK_MB) and pipelines them across a bounded pool of up to 4 staging slots, overlapping host copies with device DMAs.

📝 Summary of Changes
VerifyConcatenateAlignment previously rejected any concatenate whose concat-dim tile offset had a negative constant part (base_offset < 0). That `base_offset` is the constant part inherited from surrounding ops (e.g. a pad's edge_padding_low), so a negative value is legitimate: it only means the anchor tile reaches before the concatenated tensor and the out-of-range prefix is masked.

Replace the sign-based rejection with a sign-agnostic, phase-correct boundary-alignment check:
  - Keep the true (possibly negative) `base_offset`. The operand-location loop naturally selects operand 0 for a negative anchor, and `variable_step = offset_expr - base_offset` collapses to `d[*]*tile_size` for any sign, so the multiple-of-tile-size check stays valid.

In the `%concatenate.42.10 ` op `%param_2.543` (`bf16[1,3072,1,64]`) is used as __both__ operand 0 and operand 1 of the concatenate along dim-3, doubling the tail dimension 64 → 128.

When `--xla_gpu_experimental_enable_tiling_propagation=true` propagates a tile backwards through the concatenate to determine what slice of `%param_2.543` to load, it computes per-operand offsets independently:

| Operand slot | Maps output tile `[..., T : T+S]` to input offset |
|---|---|
| slot 0 | `T` |
| slot 1 | `T − 64` |

Because both slots alias the __same SSA value__, the tiler tries to unify both required windows into a single tile for `%param_2.543`. When `T = 0` (tile starts at the beginning of the concat output), the slot-1 input offset is `0 − 64 = −64`, which is negative and triggers the FAILED_PRECONDITION assert in `tile_propagation.cc`.

The `if (base_offset < 0)` guard in `VerifyConcatenateAlignment`  that reject tile when the offset at d=0 is negative, is a too conservative condition, as negative offsets are valid cases in real-world scenarios that do not necessarily lead to the tile being rejected; however, the alignment condition must be evaluated before determining the validity of the tile’s configuration. This PR therefore aims to do so.

PR #48560: [XLA:CPU] Support scatter and small while loops inside sort comparators

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/48560

## 📝 Summary of Changes

Fixes #47370.

A scatter inside a sort comparator aborts the CPU compiler with
`ir_emitter.cc:3501 Check failed: 1 == assigned_buffers.size() (1 vs. 2)`.
Two things go wrong. Since the fusion emitter took over scatters, scatters
are only lowered when they end up in a fusion, but no fusions are formed
inside embedded computations (comparators, reducers), so the scatter reaches
the legacy nested emitter which never supported it. And even if the scatter is
expanded, the expansion produces a while loop plus in-place
dynamic-update-slices, and the legacy emitter can handle neither in a
comparator: the thread-local buffer code insists on one value per allocation
(that is the CHECK above, also hit by a plain dynamic-update-slice in a
comparator), and a while loop in a comparator dies in `EmitGlobalCall`.

The change:

- `ScatterExpander` takes an optional `extra_filter` (just forwarded to
  `OpExpanderPass`). The CPU pipeline uses it to expand scatters whose parent
  computation is embedded, so they never reach the emitter.
- New CPU pass `EmbeddedWhileLoopUnroller` (`xla/backends/cpu/transforms/`)
  runs right after the expansion and fully unrolls while loops that live in
  embedded computations, using `WhileLoopUnroller` with its default
  thresholds. Loops it cannot unroll are left alone (they fail the same way
  as before).
- `IrEmitter::EmitThreadLocalBufferPointer` accepts a thread-local allocation
  with several aliased values. Thread-local allocations are created with
  `NewAllocation(HloBuffer)`, so every value spans the whole allocation and
  one alloca is exactly right for all of them (a CHECK keeps the byte sizes
  honest).
- `IrEmitter` returns `Unimplemented` instead of CHECK-failing in
  `EmitGlobalCall` when an embedded computation calls a global one
  (`HandleCall`, `HandleWhile`, `HandleConditional`).

Known limitations, both fail with a status now instead of an abort: loops
above the unroller's default threshold (more than 64 scatter indices) are
left alone and get `Unimplemented` from the emitter, and a scatter that is
only transitively embedded (say inside a while body in a comparator) is not
expanded and hits the existing `Scatter is not implemented on CPUs` error.

With that, scatter, variadic scatter, dynamic-update-slice and small while
loops all work inside comparators and produce the correct sort order.

The exact module from the issue additionally needs #48160: the expander's
bounds check leaves a `reduce` in the comparator whose reducer the emitter
never emits (#47366). With both changes it compiles and runs.

## 🎯 Justification

The input is valid HLO (it runs on the interpreter) and crashes the process
instead of compiling or returning an error. The same thread-local CHECK also
fires for an ordinary dynamic-update-slice in a comparator, which is a more
plausible real-world shape than the fuzzer-found scatter.

🐛 Bug Fix

- `//xla/service/cpu/tests:cpu_edge_cases_test_cpu`: four new executing
  tests (scatter, variadic scatter, dynamic-update-slice, while loop in a
  sort comparator), all abort at head and pass with this change, plus one

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/50178

**Stacked PR 3/5** splitting #48985 into reviewable layers. Stacked on #50177: the base branch is `shawnw/bfc-growth-2-reserved-suballocator`, so this PR shows only its own commit. When #50177 lands, this PR is rebased onto `main` and re-targeted.

| # | PR | Title |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | #50176 | [XLA:GPU] StreamExecutor: VA reservation and physical allocation APIs sharing the executor's VMM options |
| 2 | #50177 | [XLA:GPU] DeviceMemAllocator: reserved-arena mode that maps physical memory on demand |
| 3 | #50178 | [XLA:TSL] BFC: grow spatially partitioned pools within a reserved arena |
| 4 | #50179 | [XLA:GPU] PJRT: typed MemFraction memory policy with START-CAP grammar |
| 5 | #50180 | [XLA:GPU] PJRT: enable BFC growth for growable memory fractions |

---

📝 Summary of Changes

With `Options::allow_growth` and `enable_spatial_partitioning` both set, BFC allocates `initial_region_bytes` up front and lets upper-end (default memory) requests extend the arena through the suballocator up to `total_memory`. Lower-end (collective) requests stay confined to the initial region so symmetric NCCL window offsets never move. Contiguous extensions coalesce with the region's free tail.

```text
base                               P                  M          C
| S(1) ---> | free gap | old S(0)  | free | <--- S(0) | unmapped |
                                   |<- new backing -->|
```

`Extend` computes the smallest extension that lets the request fit after coalescing with the tail (smaller than the request when the tail helps, larger when alignment padding is needed) and uses it as the floor of the capacity check and the backpedal loop, while the target stays the usual growth size. Attempts are sized in whole suballocator granules so a shrunken retry is never padded back to a size that just failed. A short extension that lands in a separate region is returned. The initial region backpedals like a fixed pool when memory is short, with a warning, and the lower-end limit is the size actually obtained. `AllocationRegion` tracks its last chunk, so no chunk-list walks remain.

🎯 Justification

Core of the growable pool. No production code sets `allow_growth` with spatial partitioning yet, so there is no behavior change.

✨ New Feature (dormant until wired up)

`//xla/tsl/framework:bfc_allocator_test`: growth only after gap misses, fixed lower capacity, normal growth sizing, backpedal and failure recovery, contiguous coalescing across the old end, granularity-aware backpedal, growth at a physical limit below the virtual cap, non-adjacent short extensions, alignment padding, initial-region backpedal.

PR #50101: [ROCm] Emit dynamic-slice copy thunks only on CUDA Ampere+

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/50101

## 📝 Summary of Changes

Gate `AnalyzeDynamicSliceCopyFusion` / `EmitDynamicSliceCopyFusion` in `ThunkEmitter::EmitFusion` on CUDA Ampere+, so ROCm no longer emits `DynamicSliceFusionV2Thunk` for dynamic-slice / dynamic-update-slice copy fusions and falls back to the regular fusion emitter.

## 🎯 Justification

#44044 (`f4f4f9c984`) replaced `FusionDynamicMemcpyRewriter` with an analysis consumed directly by `ThunkEmitter::EmitFusion`. The rewriter lived in `FusionDispatchPipeline`, which `gpu_compiler.cc` only runs for CUDA Ampere+; the new call site in `EmitFusion` has no platform check, so since that commit ROCm also emits `DynamicSliceFusionV2Thunk`.

On ROCm that thunk cannot be recorded into a command buffer: `IsConvertible(DynamicSliceFusionV2Thunk)` requires
`SupportsMovedChildCommands`, which returns false for any non-CUDA device (`command_buffer_conversion_pass.cc`). Every DS/DUS copy in a `while` body (e.g. `lax.scan` over layers) therefore splits the enclosing command buffer.
The result is many more command-buffer launches per step, which measurably slows multi-GPU steps that have no collective in them.

## 🚀 Kind of Contribution

🐛 Bug Fix, ⚡️ Performance Improvement for ROCm ( basically restores lost perf ).

## 🧪 Unit Tests

- New `SupportsDynamicSliceCopyThunks(const se::DeviceDescription&)` in
  `dynamic_slice_copy.h` is used by both `ThunkEmitter::EmitFusion` and the
  `DynamicSliceCopyFusionAsyncWrapper` gate in `GpuCompiler`. `SupportsDynamicSliceCopyThunksTest` in
  `dynamic_slice_copy_test.cc` pins it: A100/H100 true, pre-Ampere CUDA and
  MI210/MI350 false.
- `GpuCopyTest.UseMemcpyForDynamicSlice` / `UseMemcpyForDynamicUpdateSlice`
  now check per platform: no kernel where copy thunks are emitted, a kernel otherwise. This pins the platform split.
- `UseMemcpyForDynamicUpdateSliceWithBitcasts`  `UseMemcpyForDynamicUpdateSliceWithOutOfBoundsConstantOffsets` and
  `DynamicUpdateSliceOffsetTable` check kernel counts only where copy thunks are emitted (`...WithBitcasts` and `...WithOutOfBoundsConstantOffsets` also check that a kernel is emitted otherwise), and compare numerics on every platform.

[SPARK-59975][SQL] Handle all-null partial and final tuple/theta intersection aggregates

### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

Previously `theta_intersection_agg`, `tuple_intersection_agg_double` and
`tuple_intersection_agg_integer` threw an error when all input sketches were NULL,
even for group by, when a single all-NULL group caused the entire query to fail, even if
other groups contained valid sketches. The same happens, even without NULL sketches,
for a global aggregate with an empty input partition or zero input rows, and for a query
with two or more DISTINCT aggregates (`RewriteDistinctAggregates` replaces the regular
aggregates' inputs with NULL on the expanded rows).

The error could also occur during partial aggregation when one partition contained
only NULL sketches for a group, even if another partition contained valid sketches
for that same group.

This change serializes untouched intermediate states as NULL and skips them
during merging. Final evaluation returns an empty sketch when all inputs for
the group are NULL.

We changed so that:
- `serialize()`: return an empty byte array for an untouched intersection state instead of calling `getResult()`, which throws
- `merge()`: skip untouched incoming states or untouched incoming states, real empty sketches still participate in the intersection

### Why are the changes needed?

Intersection aggregates currently throw when a partial aggregation receives only
null sketches, which can fail a query even when another partition has a valid sketch
for the same group. Untouched partials should be passed through as null and only
an all-null final result should become an empty sketch.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

Yes. `theta_intersection_agg`, `tuple_intersection_agg_double` and
`tuple_intersection_agg_integer` now return an empty sketch for all-null
input instead of throwing. Null-only partials also no longer cause otherwise
valid distributed aggregations to fail.

### How was this patch tested?

Added unit tests for the updated serialization, deserialization, merge and
final-evaluation behavior and integration tests covering:
- all-NULL input across partitions returns an empty final sketch
- grouped input correctly handles both an all-NULL group and a
group with a NULL-only partition plus a valid-sketch partition
- a global aggregate with an empty input partition and with zero input rows
- a query with multiple DISTINCT aggregates
- a window aggregate whose frame contains only NULL sketches

[SPARK-57324][SQL][UDF] Surface external UDF terminal metrics

### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

Add a typed `ExecutionMetrics` protobuf to the external UDF worker protocol's `FinishResponse` and `CancelResponse`, as a new `execution_metrics` field at the end of each message. The existing free-form `metrics` map stays at field 1, so workers and engines built against either version keep working together.

The message defines optional fields for row, batch, and payload-byte counts plus wall-clock and CPU timings, and documents what each field measures: its direction, unit, and interval, including which timers are wait times. It also carries two per-stream maxima -- the worker's slowest and most CPU-intensive data unit -- which the engine cannot recover from the summed timings. Each terminal response carries one cumulative snapshot for its `Execute` stream: final totals on finish and partial totals on acknowledged cancellation. An absent field means unavailable, while a present zero means measured zero.

Create corresponding SQL metrics and aggregate the fields present in the terminal snapshot when a worker session closes. Values outside Spark's signed `Long` metric range are ignored. Count metrics start at zero, so a count that a worker omits adds nothing to the SQL UI total. Worker session creation is a separate `createUDFWorkerSession` hook, so tests can replace the worker while running the production close-and-record lifecycle.

### Why are the changes needed?

The protocol currently exposes terminal metrics as string keys and values, and `ExternalUDFExec` discards them. A typed protobuf gives worker implementations generated, type-safe accessors and gives the engine a stable contract for exposing equivalent measurements consistently.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

Yes, within unreleased `master`. External UDF physical operators expose typed worker execution metrics in the SQL UI and event data. Spark reads these metrics from the new `execution_metrics` field; the `metrics` map is unchanged and remains worker-defined.

3. Makes `PlanMerger` treat two derivations of the same nested ordering as different, so scan merging can be declined.

[SPARK-59824][SQL] Guard top-level StringType/BinaryType inputs to pickle Python UDFs

### What changes were proposed in this pull request?
**Problem**
For non-Arrow Python UDFs, Spark evaluates the UDF input expressions and serializes the projected row using Java conversion followed by pickle serialization.

A single row can contain a very large string or binary value. Because batching cannot split an individual row, converting and pickling it may create several large in-memory copies and cause an executor OOM before the row reaches the Python worker.

Existing batch-size limits do not protect against this case.

**Proposed change**
Add an optional row-size guard for pickle-based Python UDFs.

The guard should:
- Run after UDF input expressions are projected, so computed values such as cast, concat, and substring are measured.
- Run before Java conversion and pickle serialization.
- Estimate the payload size of supported top-level variable-width arguments, initially strings and binary values.
- Fail with a structured error when the estimated size exceeds a configurable threshold based on executor heap.
- Introduce no per-row overhead when disabled or when the projected schema has no supported variable-width arguments.

Pls note that: Nested arrays, maps, and structs are intentionally excluded initially to avoid a recursive traversal of every input value.

### Why are the changes needed?
Avoid single giant row crashing executors.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?
Yes.

Previously, a single oversized input row for a pickle-serialized Python UDF was converted and serialized without a row-level size check, potentially causing executor OOM or a Python worker crash.

This PR adds an opt-in guard that checks the combined payload size of top-level string and binary arguments after projection and before conversion and pickling. If the configured executor-heap fraction is exceeded, the query fails with
UDF_LIMITS.ROW_SIZE.

The guard is disabled by default, so default behavior remains unchanged. This capability is new relative to both released Spark versions and the current master branch.

[SPARK-60084][SQL] Fix PlanMerger losing a reused filter attribute before the aggregate

### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

`PlanMerger.mergeNamedExpressions` appended the new plan's propagated filter attribute only when it was a fresh alias. A reused one (`isNew = false`) was assumed to be in the merged expression list already.

This PR appends the new plan's filter attribute whenever the list doesn't output it yet. It also drops the `isNew` flag from `TryMergeResult.newPlanFilter`, because nothing reads it any more.

The reuse lookup in the tagged `(Filter, Filter)` branch now only matches the filter aliases that the merged `Filter` references. Before, a computed column with the same expression as the new plan's filter could be reused, and the merged `Filter` would drop that plan's rows.

### Why are the changes needed?

The assumption doesn't hold. A merge round can fold a filter attribute into another filter alias, and then only the new alias is carried up to the aggregate. A later round that reuses the original attribute ends up with an aggregate `FILTER` on an attribute its child doesn't output:

```sql
SET spark.sql.optimizer.mergeSubplans.filterPropagation.symmetricFilterPropagation.enabled=true;
SET spark.sql.optimizer.mergeSubplans.filterPropagation.throughJoin.enabled=true;

CREATE TABLE t USING parquet AS SELECT * FROM VALUES
  (1, 1, 10), (1, 2, 3), (2, 1, 7), (2, 2, 9), (3, 1, 9), (3, 2, 6) AS v(a, b, c);

SELECT
  (SELECT sum(l.a) FROM t l LEFT JOIN t r ON l.a = r.a WHERE l.b = 1),
  (SELECT max(l.a) FROM t l LEFT JOIN t r ON l.a = r.a WHERE l.b = 2 AND coalesce(r.c, 10) > 5),
  (SELECT count(*) FROM t l LEFT JOIN t r ON l.a = r.a WHERE l.b = 2);
```

```
[INTERNAL_ERROR_ATTRIBUTE_NOT_FOUND] Could not find propagatedFilter_3#179 in [sum#141L,max#182,count#145L,a#6,propagatedFilter_5#181,propagatedFilter_4#180]. SQLSTATE: XX000
```

What happens there:
1. Merging the 2nd subquery into the 1st aliases `l.b = 2` on the left side of the join.
2. The 2nd subquery's post-join `coalesce(r.c, 10) > 5` folds that alias into a new `AND` alias.
3. The 3rd subquery reuses the `l.b = 2` alias, but the `Project` under the aggregate only outputs the new one.

This was found while reviewing #59161, which runs into the same problem through its new join `AND`.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

Yes. The query above now returns `12, 3, 6` instead of failing. It needs both configs above, which are off by default. The bug is in 4.2.0.

### How was this patch tested?

New tests in `MergeSubplansSuite` (merged plans, including the computed column case) and `PlanMergingSuite` (end to end). They all fail without the fix. `MergeSubplansSuite` and `PlanMergingSuite` pass.

[SPARK-59995][SQL] Drop sort orders that hold a partition transform from a V2 scan's output ordering

### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

`DataSourceV2ScanExecBase.outputOrdering` now drops every sort order that holds a partition transform (`TransformExpression`):
- in a reported ordering, a transform ends the leading run of sort orders the scan keeps, like a sort order over a pruned column;
- a transform on a partition key is dropped too, while a sort order on another partition key still holds after it, since each partition holds a single key;
- in an ordering the scan derives from its partition keys, the transform keys are left out.

Dropping them loses nothing today when Spark can call the transform's function, since no operator then requires an ordering over the transform. The write path sorts by the function call instead (`DistributionAndOrderingUtils`). Dropping them is also a safe way to handle a transform Spark cannot evaluate, and it saves comparisons nobody uses. If an ordering over a transform becomes a real requirement, this needs to be revisited.

The k-way merge of `GroupPartitionsExec` now also builds its comparator with `RowOrdering.create`, like `SortExec`. It still generates code, and falls back to interpreted evaluation when that fails. It is still built on the executor, at the first comparison. `LazyCodeGenOrdering` is renamed `LazyRowOrdering` to match.

The docs of `spark.sql.sources.v2.bucketing.partitionKeyOrdering.enabled`, its 4.4 migration note and the `SupportsReportOrdering` Javadoc now say that partition transforms are left out. The `BoundFunction` Javadoc now names the scan merge, instead of a retained reported ordering, as what a semantic `equals` is needed for.

### Why are the changes needed?

With `spark.sql.sources.v2.bucketing.preserveOrderingOnCoalesce.enabled` on, `GroupPartitionsExec` can coalesce partitions with a k-way merge over its child's ordering (SPARK-55715). The merge compares rows with generated code (`LazyCodeGenOrdering`). A `TransformExpression` generates no code. So when the ordering contained a partition transform, such as `years(arrive_time)`, the task failed:
```
[INTERNAL_ERROR] Cannot generate code for expression: transformexpression(org.apache.spark.sql.connector.catalog.functions.YearsFunction$..., input[2, timestamp, true], None) SQLSTATE: XX000
```

The ordering can contain a transform in two ways:
- the source reports it via `SupportsReportOrdering`, e.g. `[id, name, years(arrive_time)]`;
- the scan derives it from its partition keys (SPARK-56241), e.g. `[id, years(arrive_time)]`.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

Yes.
- A query that k-way merges over a transform used to fail with the error above. Now it returns its rows. The merge still runs when the sort orders the scan keeps satisfy the parent.
- A sort order on a partition key after a transform can now lead the scan's ordering. For example, with partition keys `[years(ts), id]` the scan reports `[id]` instead of `[years(ts), id]`. So a sort on `id` right above the scan, e.g. from `sortWithinPartitions("id")`, is no longer needed. The new ordering can also turn a hash aggregate into a sort aggregate, since `spark.sql.execution.replaceHashWithSortAgg` keys off the scan's ordering. For example, `SELECT id, max(ts) FROM t GROUP BY id` over the partition keys `[years(ts), id]` now plans its partial aggregate as a `SortAggregateExec`.
- The failure exists since 4.2.0, which has both the k-way merge (SPARK-55715) and the key-derived ordering (SPARK-56241). It needs `spark.sql.sources.v2.bucketing.preserveOrderingOnCoalesce.enabled`, which is off by default on every branch. The derived case also needs `spark.sql.sources.v2.bucketing.partitionKeyOrdering.enabled`, which defaults to true only on master and branch-4.x.

### How was this patch tested?

- New tests in `KeyGroupedPartitioningSuite`:
  - "a scan's output ordering drops sort orders that hold a partition transform" checks the three cases above, and that a sort on the kept key needs no `SortExec`;
  - two k-way merge tests, one for each way above. Each checks the answer, that the plan k-way merges, and the ordering it merges over. They fail on master with the error above. The derived one uses `days`, a function Spark cannot call.
- New test in `GroupPartitionsExecSuite`: "the k-way merge ordering falls back to interpreted evaluation". It serializes a `LazyRowOrdering` over a transform, which generates no code, and compares rows with it. It fails without the fallback.
- The SPARK-56321 test in `WriteDistributionAndOrderingSuite` now checks the reported ordering, and that the output ordering drops its transform.

[SPARK-59671][SQL] Validate a co-partitioned pair by its children's pairing

### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

`ValidateRequirements` judges a multi-child co-partitioned operator (a join, a cogroup) on the pairing of its children: every side offers the layouts it actually reports (`PartitioningCollection.specsForPairing` — no key deduped, none re-sorted), and one member of the first side has to pair with every other side (`KeyedShuffleSpec.isCompatibleWith`). `validateInternal` keeps the base loop; for a multi-child clustered operator the per-child distribution clause is delegated to that pairing, which asks each side the same question plus the alignment stamp and sinks on an empty side, so nothing is lost by the delegation. The ordering clause stays per child.

For that question to be decidable, a keyed layout that repeats partition keys has to say where the repetition comes from, so `KeyLayout` carries `ungroupingOrigin: Option[UngroupingOrigin]`, a sealed ADT with three values:

- `SPLIT_FOR_JOIN` / `REPLICATED_FOR_JOIN` — the two complementary sides of a partially clustered alignment. For a key, a partition holding part of it on the spread side holds all of it on the repeating side, so pairing the two index by index loses no match, and that split is the whole of the pair's soundness.
- `SPLIT_FOR_ORDERING` — the spread `EnsureRequirements.resolveChild` builds for an `OrderedDistribution`. It pairs with nothing.

Producers and carriers:

- Only `EnsureRequirements` stamps, at the two sites that build these shapes; the alignment stamp stays gated by the existing `canDuplicateLeftSide`/`canDuplicateRightSide` checks, so a `FullOuter` join gets no spread pair and a `LeftOuter` repeats its right side or groups. A `SortMergeAsOfJoinExec` gets no keyed alignment at all: its matches are read in the order within a partition, which neither side preserves.
- `GroupPartitionsExec` drops the `distributePartitions` constructor field and derives the routing from the origin (`ungroupingOrigin.exists(_ != REPLICATED_FOR_JOIN)`); `computeGrouping` writes the node's *own* origin into the layout it builds, replacing any claim the child's layout carried, and only while the computed shape actually stays ungrouped: a grouping that settles every key spends the stamp the way `toGrouped` does, so a grouped layout never carries a claim.
- Carriers keep one agreed claim: `toGrouped` spends the origin, `concat` and `fromPartitionings` keep it only where every member carries the same, and `withKeyPositionsFor` forwards its node's own.

Consumers:

- `KeyedPartitioning.satisfies`: a clustering asks that a key's rows share a partition, which no ungrouped layout gives on its own, so the clustering arm stays the base `isGrouped && keysSatisfy`, and the stamp is read only where a pair is judged (`pairsUngrouped`, feeding `specsForPairing`; the role check in `isCompatibleWith`). An ordering pairs nothing, so an ungrouped layout answers it on the keys alone, with the keys checked to ascend in the sequence the ordering reads (`keysSortedFor`, a construction shared with `resolveChild`'s keep-versus-spread decision).
- `KeyedShuffleSpec.isCompatibleWith`: an ungrouped pair is compatible only as one spread side against one repeating side.

### Why are the changes needed?

https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-59671

The validator compared children through `createShuffleSpec` — the planner-facing view (keys deduped and re-sorted) of what a node about to be inserted would report. Two failure modes follow:

1. **Sound plans fail as a whole.** A partially clustered alignment leaves both of its sides ungrouped on purpose, so a finished plan never matches the planner-facing view; `AdaptiveSparkPlanExec.optimizeQueryStage` validates the whole candidate plan and one unsatisfied node reverts every `AQEShuffleReadRule` application in it. An aggregate's shuffle read then stays uncoalesced because a join elsewhere in the plan is aligned, e.g. (with `spark.sql.sources.v2.bucketing.partiallyClusteredDistribution.enabled=true`) a chain of same-key joins over bucketed tables, or — with `sorting.enabled` — `(SELECT id FROM t ORDER BY id) UNION ALL (SELECT count(*) FROM s GROUP BY k)`, where the sort branch keeps a keyed scan's splits and no node settles them.

2. **Admitting ungrouped layouts without the producer's fact is a wrong-results hazard.** `AQEShuffleReadExec` with mapper partition specs reports `s.child.outputPartitioning` — the layout from *before* the shuffle, e.g. a scan whose key `1` sits in two splits (`[1, 1, 2]`). Two such sides agree key by key and on the count while neither holds a key's whole group; a join consuming them as aligned zips mapper `i` against mapper `i` and loses every match that crosses mappers (3 rows instead of 5 in the regression test). With the origin on the layout, such a read carries no stamp: it satisfies no clustering, validation fails, and AQE reverts the local read — the join consumes the whole shuffle read, as on base.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

No change to query results. Plans regain the AQE shuffle-read optimizations (partition coalescing, local reads where sound) that a plan holding a deliberately ungrouped layout used to revert stage-wide; one such layout — an ungrouped keyed one under an `OrderedDistribution`, which pairs no partition — now satisfies it, where grouping was required before. Ungrouped layouts are otherwise consumed no more widely than on base: a clustering still refuses one unless a producer vouched for the shape.

### How was this patch tested?

Tests were added/rewritten at four levels:

- End-to-end (`KeyGroupedPartitioningSuite`): `a partially clustered join leaves AQE's shuffle coalescing alone`; `a three-table chain keeps its AQE coalescing` (also pins the complementary stamps below the joins and the claim-free join outputs); `an AQE local read over a split scan does not lose matches` (the data-consistency regression, with final-plan assertions: three shuffle stages, no local read reporting a keyed layout, no grouping node over a partial read); `an ungrouped sort branch leaves AQE's shuffle coalescing alone`; `an aggregate over a left outer join's spread side groups it` (a single-child consumer of the side `ShuffledJoin.outputPartitioning` reports verbatim must settle it, not read its stamp).
- Producer gates (`EnsureRequirementsSuite`): `an ordering spread carries its own reason and serves only the ordering`; `the alignment stamps one repeating side, only where the join type may` (Inner, both LeftOuter picks, FullOuter); `an as-of join gets no keyed alignment, so its sides shuffle`.
- Pairing rules (`ValidateRequirementsSuite`, 11 SPARK-59671 tests): the role rules, count/order/hashed-side refusals, cogroup, collapsed layouts, ordering-versus-pairing.
- Layout mechanics (`ShuffleSpecSuite`): `the specs a side offers are the layouts it reports`; `carriers keep one agreed origin and grouping spends it`; `an ordering reads sorted keys, a clustering reads the pairing` (both halves of the ordering gate: an unsorted ungrouped layout and an unsorted grouped one answer false). `GroupPartitionsExecSuite`: `the output claim is the node's own, never inherited`; `an alignment that settles every key spends its stamp`.

[SPARK-59962][SQL] Inline common expressions in a command instead of pre-evaluating them under it

### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

`RewriteWithExpression` pre-evaluates a common expression's definition that is referenced more than once and is not cheap in a `Project` over the first child whose output covers the definition's references. That assumes the operator evaluates its expressions over its children's rows, and a command does not, nor does a `Call`, whose arguments `InvokeProcedures` expects to find foldable over its `ResolvedProcedure`. A CHECK constraint added by ALTER TABLE is stored as a V2 predicate built from the optimized expression, and a group-based DELETE pushes its condition down to the scan and reuses it for runtime group filtering, so after the rewrite these read a `_common_expr_N` column that only the added `Project` produces. CREATE TABLE, REPLACE TABLE and a DELETE on a table that deletes by filters are planned only over a `ResolvedIdentifier` or a V2 scan relation, and find the `Project` there instead.

This adds a case for a `Command` or a `Call` to the rule that substitutes every deterministic definition, and any definition read once, at its references. A row-level write (`ReplaceData`, `WriteDelta`) gets it for its `condition` only: its `groupFilterCondition` is read only by the runtime group filter, which puts it in a filter over the table and optimizes it there, so a `With` in it is treated as one in a conditional branch, inlined only where memoizing gains nothing. Analysis rejects a nondeterministic expression in every command except `CreateVariable`, and a nondeterministic definition read twice that did reach the case would keep its `With`. A `With` in a conditional branch of a command is inlined as well, since a `With` translates to no source predicate. `CreateVariable` still goes to the case SPARK-59954 added, which comes first: its default is evaluated rather than stored, so a definition there is inlined only where memoizing gains nothing.

`inlineDefsThatGainNothing` is split so the new case reuses its substitution, and `canSubstitute` takes a flag that skips its cost check for it.

### Why are the changes needed?

With default settings, NULLIF or BETWEEN over a first operand that is not cheap breaks these commands and CALL:

```sql
-- InMemoryTableCatalog as testcat
CREATE TABLE testcat.g (a INT, b INT GENERATED ALWAYS AS (nullif(a + 1, 3)));
-- [INTERNAL_ERROR] ... No plan for CreateTable ...
--   +- Project [a, b, (a + 1) AS _common_expr_0]
--      +- ResolvedIdentifier ..., g, [a, b]
-- CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE fails the same way

DELETE FROM testcat.t WHERE (a + b) BETWEEN 0 AND 4;
-- [INTERNAL_ERROR] Unexpected table relation: Project [a, b, (a + b) AS _common_expr_1] ...

-- group-based row-level table partitioned by dep
DELETE FROM rowcat.p WHERE (id + pk) BETWEEN 2 AND 4;
-- [INTERNAL_ERROR_ATTRIBUTE_NOT_FOUND] Could not find _common_expr_4 in [dep]

CALL cat.ns.sum(nullif((SELECT 5), 3), 1);
-- [INTERNAL_ERROR] Unexpected plan for optimized CALL statement

ALTER TABLE testcat.t ADD CONSTRAINT c1 CHECK (nullif(a + b, 3) > 0);
-- succeeds, but the V2 predicate stored in the catalog is
-- CASE WHEN _common_expr_1 = 3 THEN NULL ELSE _common_expr_1 > 0 END
-- and every later write fails with UNRESOLVED_COLUMN on _common_expr_1
```

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

Yes. The CREATE TABLE and CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE above succeed and INSERT computes the generated column. The DELETE on `testcat.t` reports that the table cannot delete by `[(a + b) >= 0, (a + b) <= 4]` instead of an internal error, so a source that accepts those predicates can run it. The group-based DELETE deletes the matching rows. The CALL returns 6. Writes to the table after the ALTER TABLE enforce the check. A definition referenced twice in the expression of any command but DECLARE VARIABLE, or in a CALL argument, now appears at both references, as it does with `spark.sql.alwaysInlineCommonExpr=true`, and nested NULLIF or BETWEEN compound the copies. Each copy is evaluated wherever the expression is: a CHECK predicate stored by ALTER TABLE at every later write, and a CALL argument when it is folded, so an impure function such as `aes_encrypt` over literals in a CALL argument is folded once per copy. In the runtime group filter of a row-level write, a definition that is not cheap is memoized instead.

### How was this patch tested?

- `RewriteWithExpressionSuite`: a DELETE condition holding a `With`, directly and in a conditional branch, comes out inlined with no `Project` under the command; a nondeterministic definition keeps its `With` when read twice and is inlined when read once; and a `DECLARE VARIABLE` default keeps a `With` over a definition that is deterministic but not cheap, which the new case would inline.
- `DataSourceV2SQLSuiteV1Filter`: `DELETE ... WHERE (id + p) BETWEEN 0 AND 4` on a table that cannot delete by it fails with `Cannot delete from table ... where [...]` listing both comparisons over the table's columns.
- `DeleteFromTableSuiteBase`: the same shape of condition deletes the matching rows on the group-based and delta-based row-level tables, a group-based delete copies only the rows of the groups the runtime group filter keeps, and its condition has no `With` while its group filter condition keeps one.
- `UpdateTableSuiteBase`: an UPDATE with that shape of condition updates the matching row, its condition has no `With` and its group filter condition keeps one, and on the group-based tables it copies no rows, as the runtime group filter keeps only the group of that row. A condition that folds to true leaves a true group filter condition and updates every row.
- `GeneratedColumnWriteSuite`: a table with `c INT GENERATED ALWAYS AS (nullif(a + b, 3))` is created by CREATE TABLE and then replaced by CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE, and INSERT computes `c` after each.
- `ProcedureSuite`: `CALL cat.ns.sum(nullif((SELECT 5), 3), 1)` returns 6.
- `CheckConstraintSuite`: after `ALTER TABLE ... ADD CONSTRAINT c1 CHECK (nullif(id + 1, 3) > 0)`, an INSERT the check accepts succeeds and one it rejects fails with CHECK_CONSTRAINT_VIOLATION; it passes with `SPARK_ANSI_SQL_MODE=false` as well.

All of them fail without the change except the two delta-based DELETE runs, which were not affected, and the `DECLARE VARIABLE` case, which passes on master and fails if a `CreateVariable` reaches the new case. The UPDATE runs fail only because master inlines their group filter condition; the UPDATE itself works there.

[SPARK-33301][SQL] Split a large CASE WHEN into methods under whole-stage codegen

### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

Under whole-stage codegen, `CodegenContext.splitExpressionsWithCurrentInputs` never split (`// TODO: support whole stage codegen`), so every branch of a `CASE WHEN` went into the operator's method. Outside a stage the branches are split into methods that take the input row. Inside a stage the inputs are local variables of the operator's method, and which of them a piece of code reads cannot be told from the code strings. This PR splits a `CASE WHEN` inside a stage, and only when the stage needs it.

**One input collector.** A private `CodegenContext.collectInputs` walks the expressions a piece of code was generated from and returns the locals it reads, or `None` when no method can take them. An `InputPolicy` records where its three callers differ: the whole-stage split, `getLocalInputVariableValues` (subexpressions, aggregates, `ExpandExec`), and `CommonExprSlots.methodArgs` (`With`). It replaces the two walks that existed before and the third that #59069 added. Under the whole-stage policy, the walk:
- takes the evaluated input variables of `currentVars`;
- takes `INPUT_ROW` only where the code reads it, including through a `CommonExpressionRef` whose definition became a method taking the row (that decision is now recorded when it is made);
- takes a subexpression state's value without descending below it;
- reads a slot of a compacted mutable state array as a field. With the split on this holds under every policy and in every stage: a slot counts as the field it is when code moves into a method. An operator's method that took it as a parameter, and failed to compile, now compiles; a `With` definition reading one, which stayed inline, gets its `computeCommonExpr` method. This fixes a stage whose large common subexpression reads such a slot, such as an UNPIVOT's string output: on master its `subExpr` method takes `UTF8String expand_mutableStateArray_0[1]` as a parameter, fails to compile, and the stage falls back;
- descends below a node whose code is its child's (`Alias`, `Collate`, an identity `Cast`) instead of refusing its state.

It refuses an input the operator has not evaluated yet, and a value no parameter can carry. `getLocalInputVariableValues` keeps its signature and its results.

**One split, with a per-block fallback.** `CaseWhen` passes each branch's code together with the expressions it came from to a new `private[sql] splitExpressionsWithSources`. The existing `splitExpressionsWithCurrentInputs` keeps its signature for external callers.
- The code is packed into blocks by `methodSplitThreshold`, as everywhere, and each block gets its own arguments.
- A block the collector refuses stays inline, in its place between the calls.
- Only when every block is refused does the `CASE WHEN` stay in one piece.

**One grouping.** The calls are grouped by the grouping of SPARK-59783 (#59042), now the only implementation, with a parameter for how many calls may stay in the calling method. Inside a stage that is 8 calls. All of a projection's outputs land in one method there, so a per-expression budget would add up: four 300-branch `CASE WHEN`s gave a 13583-byte method that HotSpot never compiles.

**The stage gate.** Splitting where the stage did not need it cost 5-15% at 64 branches on the runners: C2 compiles the unsplit method as one unit, but stops inlining partway through the chain of calls. So a stage decides per method, from its own code:
1. It generates its code in one piece, marking the code of each expression a split could take.
2. It compiles that code as a trial, which reports every method's bytecode size.
3. The methods run per row that are past `spark.sql.codegen.wholeStage.splitExpressions.methodLimit` (8000 bytes by default, HotSpot's limit for JIT-compiling a method) or `spark.sql.codegen.hugeMethodLimit` are the ones a split can help. It generates the code again with only the expressions marked in those methods split. An expression in a method the JIT compiles whole is left alone.
4. It keeps the split code when that lowers the bytes past the limit and it compiles; otherwise it runs the code in one piece. If the code in one piece does not compile at all, every expression is split where that compiles; where it does not either, the code in one piece goes to `doExecute`, which reports, falls back or throws exactly as on master.

A stage the JIT compiles whole therefore keeps the code it had before this PR, including the helper functions of a discarded subexpression pass, except where code moving into a method reads a compacted slot: it reads it as a field (see above). That workaround can go once SPARK-60021 labels `ExpandExec`'s outputs as the fields they are. The details:
- The decision is remembered by a digest of the marked code, with the class loader, the compiler, the limit and `methodSplitThreshold`, so re-executing a query skips the trial compiles. Threads that meet the stage at once wait for one decision, under a per-key lock. A split that fails to compile is warned about, its code kept in one piece, thrown under testing, and remembered; the warning carries the error only where the split's compile did not log it already; where a trial's method sizes are unknown (a compile cache hit), nothing is.
- The split calls are matched between the two generations by their expressions, with lambda variables' values ignored, and their occurrence, so a copy of a CASE WHEN in a method under the limit is not split with the one past it.
- A split generation that turns no block into a method is not compiled; the code in one piece is kept, as where no split is tried: its trial's class stays cached for `doExecute` where it compiled, and where it did not, `doExecute` compiles it again and reports the failure as on master.
- The variant not kept leaves the compile cache, so the cache holds only code that runs, and a later compile of that variant reports what it finds.
- The trial compile holds back the huge-method reports, the "Code generated in" line and the codegen metrics for the code it discards, also on the JDK compiler's worker thread, and logs an expected failure at DEBUG. The `spark.sql.codegen.logLevel` source dump is not held back, so with it on, each variant compiled is dumped.
- Recording does not pack blocks, so below the limit the gate costs about 0.04 ms per code generation on a 64-branch stage (1.60 ms against 1.56 ms without the split).

**The discarded pass.** Subexpression elimination generates the common subexpressions once without splitting, and again inside `subExpr_N` methods when they are large. A generation that splits the stage's expressions now removes the functions added by the discarded first generation. A stage kept in one piece keeps them, as on master.

`spark.sql.codegen.wholeStage.splitExpressions` (internal, on by default) turns all of this off. With it off, the generated code is exactly that of master.

### Why are the changes needed?

SPARK-33301: a large `CASE WHEN` inside a stage fails to compile. On Spark 4.2.0, one `CASE WHEN` of `n` branches over a long column,

```scala
val branches = (1 to n).map(k => s"WHEN id = $k THEN id * $k").mkString(" ")
spark.sql(s"SELECT CASE $branches ELSE 0 END AS v FROM range(10)").collect()
```

compiles at 952 branches and fails at 953 ("Code grows beyond 64 KB"). Spark then disables whole-stage codegen for the plan and runs it without. Much earlier, from 96 branches in the benchmark's shape, the stage's method is past 8000 bytes, and HotSpot never JIT-compiles it (`-XX:+DontCompileHugeMethods`), so the stage runs interpreted.

`CaseWhenCodegenBenchmark` (new; its three results files are committed), best times on GitHub runners. JDK 17 ran on an AMD EPYC 7763, JDK 21 on an AMD EPYC 9V74 and JDK 25 on an Intel Xeon Platinum 8573C, so the columns compare the arms within a JDK, not the JDKs with each other.

| shape | split as needed | not split | split always | whole stage codegen off |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| one CASE WHEN, 64 branches (6049 bytes) | 92 / 95 / 63 ms | 92 / 94 / 64 ms | 97 / 100 / 64 ms | 211 / 219 / 152 ms |
| one CASE WHEN, 96 branches (9057 bytes unsplit) | 120 / 122 / 82 ms | 3992 / 3717 / 2394 ms | 115 / 115 / 75 ms | 296 / 305 / 200 ms |
| one CASE WHEN, 300 branches | 249 / 227 / 162 ms | 11854 / 12083 / 7043 ms | 232 / 216 / 143 ms | 976 / 951 / 709 ms |
| four 300-branch CASE WHENs in one projection | 1099 / 868 / 589 ms | 4638 / 5173 / 3457 ms | 1042 / 760 / 505 ms | 4643 / 5172 / 3451 ms |
| a 300-branch CASE WHEN in a keyed aggregate | 262 / 270 / 191 ms | 12558 / 11943 / 6987 ms | 243 / 234 / 167 ms | 2156 / 2358 / 2165 ms |

Below 8000 bytes, "split as needed" runs the same code as "not split", and times the same: each arm's repeat ("again" in the files) is within 1 ms of it. Past it, the split is 30 to 50 times faster than the unsplit stage, which HotSpot never compiles, and 2 to 11 times faster than running without whole-stage codegen.

What splitting as needed still costs against "split always" is the code generation it repeats: a stage that splits generates its code twice per execution, once in one piece and once split. That is 5-13% on one 300-branch CASE WHEN, 5-17% on four of them in one projection, and 8-15% in the keyed aggregate. The decision is remembered by the generated code, so a query whose code carries a literal that changes on every run, such as the timestamp `current_timestamp()` becomes, decides afresh each run and pays two generations and two compiles where master pays one of each; queries without such literals compile nothing new after the first execution. Remembering the decision by a key that ignores literal values would remove both; it is left for a follow-up (SPARK-60048).

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

No, apart from the performance of such queries. Answers are the same. A large `CASE WHEN` inside a stage now compiles, and keeps the stage's methods under the JIT limit. The exceptions are blocks that read a column the operator has not evaluated yet: they stay inline, and a `CASE WHEN` all of whose blocks do so stays in one piece, as today. A stage the JIT already compiles whole is unchanged, except where code moving into a method reads a compacted slot.

### How was this patch tested?

New tests in `WholeStageCodegenSuite` (35), `CollectInputsSuite` (12, one per row of the collector's policies, and the conf off) and `CodeCompilerSuite` (1, the scanner of generated Java). Among them:
- **Splitting:** a 3000-branch `CASE WHEN` compiles inside a stage, and at 300 branches every method stays under 8000 bytes. Several large `CASE WHEN`s in one projection keep its method small.
- **The gate:** a 64-branch stage keeps its unsplit code, byte for byte, also with common subexpressions. A stage splits only the CASE WHENs in its methods past the limit: a filter's 64-branch CASE WHEN in `processNext` stays whole beside a projection's 300-branch one that splits. The trial compile reports no huge method, logs no compile time and updates no metric for the code it discards, which each test of `chooseCode`'s decisions pins by which trial's held reports it replays; the kept code reports its huge method, also after the same code was discarded in an earlier trial. `chooseCode`'s decisions are checked with the compile faked: a split kept, a larger unsplittable method beside, a split that turns no block into a method, a split that fails to compile, warned about or thrown, code in one piece that fails to compile with the split compiling, failing or splitting nothing, unknown sizes not remembered, the memo, and two threads meeting one undecided key, which decide once. With real generations, a split that turns no block into a method, beside a discarded subexpression pass's helpers, compiles nothing more. [SPARK-59674][CORE] Fix Comparison method violates its general contract in FIFOSchedulingAlgorithm

### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

`FIFOSchedulingAlgorithm.comparator` (used by `Pool.getSortedTaskSetQueue` to order `TaskSetManager`s/`Pool`s in FIFO scheduling mode) compared `priority` and `stageId` using:

```scala
math.signum(priority1 - priority2)
```

This subtraction can silently overflow when the two `Int` values are far apart (e.g. span `Int.MinValue`..`Int.MaxValue`), which flips the sign of the result and violates the `Comparator` contract (anti-symmetry/transitivity).

This PR replaces the subtraction-based `signum` comparisons with `Integer.compare`, which compares the two values directly and cannot overflow:

```scala
var res = Integer.compare(s1.priority, s2.priority)
if (res == 0) {
  res = Integer.compare(s1.stageId, s2.stageId)
}
```

### Why are the changes needed?

A broken comparator contract makes `java.util.TimSort` detect the inconsistency during the merge phase and throw, which surfaces as a driver-side failure when offering resources to executors:

```
java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: Comparison method violates its general contract!
	at java.util.TimSort.mergeHi(TimSort.java:903)
	at java.util.TimSort.mergeAt(TimSort.java:520)
	at java.util.TimSort.mergeForceCollapse(TimSort.java:461)
	at java.util.TimSort.sort(TimSort.java:254)
	at java.util.Arrays.sort(Arrays.java:1233)
	at scala.collection.SeqLike.sorted(SeqLike.scala:659)
	...
	at org.apache.spark.scheduler.Pool.getSortedTaskSetQueue(Pool.scala:109)
	at org.apache.spark.scheduler.TaskSchedulerImpl.resourceOffers(TaskSchedulerImpl.scala:440)
	at org.apache.spark.scheduler.cluster.CoarseGrainedSchedulerBackend$DriverEndpoint.makeOffers(...)
```

Once this is thrown from `resourceOffers`, resource offers stop being processed correctly, which can stall task scheduling entirely. `Integer.compare` performs a purely logical comparison and does not have this overflow failure mode, so it satisfies the `Comparator` contract for any pair of `Int` values.
